BROTHER AND SISTER MEET AFTER FIFTY YEARS. Separated When Children, Lose Sight of Each Other For Nearly Half a Century.
Cincinnati, O., Aug. 17.—[Special.]—After a lapse of nearly half a century, Col. Robert Kirkup, the well-known Cincinnati brass founder, and his sister, Mrs. Margaret Lowe, of St. Thomas, Ont., Canada, met each other Tuesday at the home of Col. Kirkup. It has been forty-eight years since the two had seen each other.

The story of the Kirkup's, following the death of their mother, is an unusual one. Nine children were in the family, but when the mother died they drifted away from the Edinburg home one at a time, until now only one is there. John Kirkup is a brass founder in Louisville, and Mrs. Marian Kirkup Simpson is also there.

Mrs. Lowe will remain in Cincinnati the remainder of the week, and will then go to Louisville, accompanied by Col. Kirkup and members of his family. A general reunion will be held there, for it is nearly sixty years since Margaret Kirkup saw her brother John, the Louisville brass founder.

THOUGHT HE WAS CHASED SO SHOT PURSUER.

George Hickerson Gets Bullet In Shoulder Through Misunderstanding.

While George Hickerson, colored, was running through Twelfth street last night at 9:45 o'clock in an effort to overtake his daughter an unknown negro turned at the corner of Tenth and Green streets and fired a bullet into Hickerson's left side. The pellet of lead struck a rid and did little damage. Hickerson walked to the office of Dr. Perry Peters, who dressed the wound. Hickerson lives at 1122 Green street. After firing the shot the unknown negro ran. Hickerson is of the opinion that the man who fired the shot thought he was being pursued by an enemy.

HORSE COMES HOME
AFTER LONG ABSENCE.

Frankfort, Ky., Aug. 17.—[Special.]—John Dickerson, a farmer, residing in Owen county near the Franklin line, was much surprised to-day to find at his barn door a horse which had strayed or been stolen from him eight years ago. The animal had not been seen in hte neighborhood since its disappearance, but shortly after it had been identified a farmer came after it, who had secured it in a trade several months ago. Several neighbors of Dickerson identified the horse as his property.

MOTHER SPILLS BOILING
STARCH ON CHILD.

Rose Risert, the ten-year-old daughter of William Risert, was severely scalded at the home of her parents, 1418 Fifteenth street, yesterday afternoon, by the bolling over of a kettle of starch. Her head, face and arms were badly burned. Dr. Philip G. Trunnell dressed the injuries.

The child was standing near her mother in the kitchen of their home, when the starch began boiling over on the stove. In her hurry to remove the kettle the mother spilled a part of its contents over her daughter's head.

MOB HAD FORMED AND WAS READY TO STRING UP NE GRO IN SHORT ORDER.
All That Prevented a Public Lynching Was the Promise That the Law Would Be Speedily Invoked—The Negro Was Charged With Attempted Criminal Assault Upon a White Girl.

Mayor Bishop. of Paris, Tex., who had been visiting in San Antonio, received a telegram yesterday calling him home on account of a threatened lynching of a negro by a mob in Paris. The negro is alleged to have made an attempt to commit a criminal assault upon Miss Daisy Collins, aged 17, daughter of E. P. Collins.

Miss Collins was awakened about 4 o'clock yesterday morning by something touching her hand, and in the dim moonlight she saw a tall negro by the side of the bed. She screamed and the man ran across the hall and through the bed-room of her parents, escaping through an open window through which he had entered. He was barefooted and in going out the window lost his hat.

The city police answered a telephone alarm and followed the tracks some distance leading to a negro cabin. They demanded admittance, and a negro ran out the back door, jumped the fence and escaped, though one of the officers shot at him. Later in the morning the county officers aided the search and about 10 o'clock Sheriff Carpenter and Marshal Minton arrested Andrew Dinwiddie, a negro, in a corn field. three miles south of town, where he was pulling fodder. The negro said he belonged near Clarksville, but that he had been in Paris since Sunday. He admitted sleeping Wednesday night in a cabin in the east side of town, a few blocks from the Collins home, but said he slept until sunrise.

A committee of citizens waited on the sheriff, demanding the negro. It was only by the promise of the sheriff that immediate legal action would be taken that a lynching was prevented. He stated that a special grand jury would be convened to investigate the matter and the committee pledged itself to aid the sheriff in enforcing the law.

During the excitement the acting mayor of Paris ordered all the saloons closed, and they remained closed for three hours, being permitted to open after the trouble had passed.

Mayor Bishop was out automobile riding in San Antonio when he received the telegram calling him home and he left for north Texas last night.

A boy located the negro's hiding place. A mob was formed. the officers were overpowered and the negro was dragged out. The crowd surged down Main street two blocks to the square, and the negro was taken on the platform of a bandstand in the center. There were several ropes ready, but hanging was delayed until Mr. Collins could come and identify the negro in the presence of the crowd.

Before this happened County Judge Love mounted a wagon near the bandstand and pleaded with the crowd to wait for full proof. His appeal reached the better sense of men and boys who had taken charge of affairs, and they finally agreed to turn the negro back to the sheriff if they were promised that after twenty-four hours he should be returned to them, if he proved to be guilty. Several reputable citizens who had taken no part in the trouble, but were standing with Judge Love agreed to this and the negro was accordingly taken to the jail and delivered to the sheriff.

CITIZENS PREVENT LYNCHING IN TEXAS Judge Makes Appeal to Thousand Persons Who Have Rope Around Neck of Negro—Assailant Is Returned to Officers.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Paris, Tex., Aug. 11.—An appeal from several prominent citizens of this city, headed by Judge Love, this afternoon prevented the bystander in a negro, who gave his name to Dinwiddie, and who was charged with an attempt to assault the 15-year-old daughter of a prominent merchant of this city.

Dinwiddie was taken from the officers about 3 o'clock this afternoon by an excited mob of about 1,400 persons. The mob moved to the public square with the intention of putting the negro to death.

The rope had been placed around the negro's neck and the lynching seemed imminent when Judge Love, accompanied by several prominent citizens, appealed to the leaders.

Within a few minutes they had convinced the leaders that there was no conclusive evidence of guilt against the negro and he was acquitted.

MOB RESENTS SURRENDER.

Many persons in the mob received the surrender of Dinwiddie, but they made no attempt to again take him from the officers.

Dinwiddie was placed in jail and Judge Love promised the mob leaders that he would be brought to a speedy trial.

The crime with which the negro is charged was attempted about 4 o'clock this morning. The young woman was awakened by the negro, who had just gained entrance to her room through an open window. She screamed and the negro jumped through the window and disappeared.

A posse was heavily organized, and at 11 o'clock Dinwiddie was arrested. He was taken to jail at once, and the citizens learned that a suspect had been captured a mob was formed, which marched to the jail and took the negro from the Sineriff.

The father of the young lady has identified Dinwiddie as the negro whom he saw fleeing from his house after being awakened by the screams of the young lady.

LOUISIANA TO HAVE SEWERS.

City Council Grants Franchise to Pittsburg Company.

REPUBLIC SPECIAL

REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Louisiana, No., Aug. 24—Louisiana will have a sewer system. For several months the question has been agitated and various plans have been discussed and considered. The City Council has voted a sewer franchise to the American Waterworks and Guaranty Company of Pittsbure Pa. This company owns the water plant here.

It will cost about $500 to put in the main sewers, and those who use sewers will pay rental. The company has thirty days in which to accept the franchise. It will accept, provided its water franchise is extended, which probably will be done.

REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

New York, Aug. 23—New York had a brand-new thrill to day when half a million persons saw Roy Knabenshue sail his airship two miles against a six-mile wind and back to the top of a tree in Central Park. Until a spark plug was torn out by catching in the aeronaut's trousers as he moved forward and back on the framework of the ship in directing its flight, he had the ship under perfect control. Had it not been for this accident, he says, he could have easily circled the Statue of Liberty or passed under and over the Brooklyn bridge—feats he promises to execute within a few days at Sixth-second street and Central Park West, where the airship is housed in a tent. Knabenshue rose at an angle of 45 degrees, only to find himself helpless to operate his driving apparatus. He had thrown the power on too suddenly, the effect of which was to throw the driving chain off.

A light breeze lifted the ship across the street and the release of a small amount of gas in the balloon let it settle easily on the West Drive. His reception there by a policeman was one of the interesting side lights of the occasion.

"Get out of here with your machine, and do it mighty quick, or you'll come along with me," he was told.

ASCENDS TO ESCAPE ARREST.

Knabenshue was no more anxious to remain than the policeman was to have him. It was a matter of only a few minutes to replace the driving chain, and once more the airship rose gracefully above the trees and sailed away amid the cheers of a crowd that had gathered.

At a sharp angle, it shot up until it had reached an altitude of about a thousand feet, when the aeronaut brought it to an even keel and headed a trifle west from south. Keeping his rubber in constant motion, as the head wind sought to turn the fish-shaped balloon from its course, which forced Knabenshue to proceed by short to drive the ship down the line of Broadway until he had reached a point 1,500 feet above Forty-second street.

By this time the streets were filled with thousands gaving excitedly at the first airship which ever floated over New York, and other thousands crowded on house-tops, all straining their eyes at the speck in control of the aeronaut.

They saw him sweep widely about on the wind, as easily as a yacht swings off to be swept before a breeze. In a course as straight and true as an arrow's flight he drove the ship due north and on a descending plane until he was only a couple of hundred feet above the heads of the crowds in the streets.

THE LATEST.

The latest reply of the Czar to President Roosevelt's compromise proposition is said to be partially responsive and at St. Petersburg there is a general feeling that all hope is not lost. President Roosevelt is in constant communication with both St. Petersburg and Tokio, and sees encouragement in the press reports from St. Petersburg. jim-lawyer-1905-08-09.A4:
NEGRO FLOGGED FOR DENOUNCING LYNCHING
Special to The Light.

Waco, Tex., Aug. 10.—A negro, named Jim Lawyer, was taken from his neighbor's home near Bruceville, this county, last night, and given a sound flogging.

This was occasioned by some statements that were made by him in condemning the whites for lynching Sank Majors. There were about twenty men who called upon Lawyer, and after hearing his statement they reported him and told him that it would be better for him to hunt other climes.

He took them at their word and left this morning.

There is still considerable feeling with reference to the lynching, and further talk by the negroes will be to their own trouble.
jim-lawyer-1905-08-09.A5:
WHIPPED BY WHITES.
Comments of Jim Lawyer, a Negro, Cause Him a Flogging.
Waco, Aug. 10.—A negro named Jim Lawyer was taken from his home near Bruceville. this county. Wednesday night and given a sound flogging. This was occasioned by some statements that were made by him in condemning the whites for lynching Sank Majors. About twenty white men called upon Lawyer, and after hearing his statement whipped him, and told him that it would be better for him to hunt other climes. He took them at their word and left Thursday.
